title: Genetic Diseases of the Kidney
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the single-gene disorders that most often reach the kidney: polycystic kidney disease, type IV collagen disease, the tumor suppressor syndromes behind renal carcinoma, Wilms tumor, and angiomyolipoma, and two metabolic disorders, cystinuria and Fabry disease. For each, it follows the chain from gene to protein to cell to the renal and extrarenal findings. Board questions usually give a pedigree, a biopsy or urine finding, or a cluster of extrarenal signs and ask for the gene, the protein, the inheritance, or the risk to a relative. If you understand what the normal protein does, the findings become predictable.
prerequisites: Mendelian inheritance, pedigree symbols, and X inactivation
Tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes, and the Knudson two-hit hypothesis
Nephron structure, the glomerular filtration barrier, and proximal tubule transport (UR-2, UR-6)
Development of the metanephros from ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme (UR-1)

connections.how: WT1 controls the conversion of metanephric mesenchyme into nephron epithelium, so its loss links Wilms tumor to genitourinary malformation.
Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha-3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen, part of the same network that is missing or defective in Alport syndrome.
The cystic diseases and Alport syndrome are taught there as pathology; this chapter supplies the gene and protein mechanisms.
VHL loss, WT1 loss, 11p15 imprinting defects, and TSC loss explain clear cell carcinoma, Wilms tumor, and angiomyolipoma.
Cystinuria is the inherited stone disease, and its solubility rules are the same ones that govern other stones.

terms.def: A single nonmotile projection from the apical surface of a tubular cell that houses signaling proteins, including the polycystins and fibrocystin.
A disease caused by defective structure or signaling of the primary cilium, such as polycystic kidney disease.
The model in which both alleles of a tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated for a lesion to form; in hereditary syndromes the first hit is inherited.
Loss of the remaining normal allele in a cell that carries one mutant allele, often by deletion of a chromosome segment.
A state in which one functional copy of a gene is not enough for normal function.
A mutation whose abnormal product interferes with the protein made from the normal allele.
Parent-of-origin gene expression set by DNA methylation in the germline, so only the maternal or only the paternal allele is active.
Inheritance of both copies of a chromosome or chromosome segment from one parent.
A transcription factor whose alpha subunit is destroyed in normal oxygen and that activates angiogenic and metabolic genes in hypoxia.
A benign, disorganized overgrowth of tissue types normally found at that site.
A disorder in which deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme lets its undegraded substrate accumulate inside cells.
Random inactivation of one X chromosome in each female cell early in development, which makes heterozygous females mosaics.

sections.title: Polycystic kidney disease: polycystins, fibrocystin, and pedigrees

blocks.text: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) replaces renal parenchyma with fluid-filled cysts derived from tubular epithelium. Autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD), about 1 in 400 to 1,000 births, is the most common inherited kidney disease and presents in adults. Autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD), about 1 in 20,000 births, presents in the fetus or infant. Both are ciliopathies: the defective proteins work at the primary cilium that each tubular cell extends into the lumen.

Polycystin-1, encoded by PKD1 on chromosome 16 (about 85% of families), is a large receptor-like membrane protein. Polycystin-2, encoded by PKD2 on chromosome 4 (about 15%), is a Ca2+-permeable cation channel. Together they are thought to sense a ciliary signal such as luminal flow and admit Ca2+. When the complex fails, intracellular Ca2+ falls and cAMP rises. In cyst epithelium cAMP drives proliferation through the B-Raf and ERK pathway and opens CFTR Cl- channels, so the cells secrete Cl- and water into the lumen; vasopressin acting on V2 receptors is a major source of this cAMP.

blocks.title: ADPKD pathogenesis
steps: Germline PKD1 or PKD2 mutation; somatic hit in one tubular cell
Polycystin complex fails at the primary cilium
Intracellular Ca2+ falls; cAMP rises
Proliferation and CFTR-driven Cl- and fluid secretion
Cyst detaches from its nephron and enlarges for decades
Compression of nephrons and vessels: renin release, nephron loss
Hypertension and progressive kidney failure
blocks.caption: Every cell carries one mutant allele, but a cyst forms only where a second somatic event drops polycystin function below a threshold.

blocks.text: Although every cell carries the mutation, cysts arise from only a small fraction of nephrons, because each cyst requires a second, somatic hit to the normal allele. Compression of neighboring tissue causes regional ischemia and renin release, so hypertension often precedes a fall in GFR. A concentrating defect appears early, and flank pain, hematuria from cyst rupture, cyst infection, and stones are common. PKD1 disease is more severe, reaching kidney failure about two decades earlier than PKD2 disease. Polycystins also act in biliary epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and connective tissue, which explains liver cysts (the most common extrarenal finding), intracranial berry aneurysms with subarachnoid hemorrhage, mitral valve prolapse, and colonic diverticula.

ARPKD requires mutation of both alleles of PKHD1 on chromosome 6, which encodes fibrocystin, a ciliary protein of collecting duct and bile duct epithelium. Dilated collecting ducts form elongated cysts that run radially toward a smooth capsule. Poor fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios and the Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, limb deformities), and malformation of the embryonic ductal plate causes congenital hepatic fibrosis with later portal hypertension.

blocks.title: ADPKD and ARPKD compared
rows: Bilaterally enlarged, cysts from all segments, bumpy surface
Bilaterally enlarged, radial collecting duct cysts, smooth surface
Berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, diverticula
Vertical: every generation, both sexes, male-to-male transmission, 50% risk per child
Horizontal: unaffected carrier parents, 25% risk per child, consanguinity raises risk
blocks.caption: About 10% of ADPKD patients have no affected parent because of a new mutation or a mildly affected parent.

blocks.title: Worked example: risk in a PKD family
blocks.text: A healthy woman's brother had ARPKD. Her parents must both be carriers. She is unaffected, so she is one of three equally likely genotypes (two carrier, one noncarrier): her carrier risk is 2/3, not 1/2. Her unrelated husband has the population carrier risk, about 1 in 70. Their child's risk is 2/3 x 1/70 x 1/4, about 1 in 420. Now suppose instead that the husband's mother has ADPKD and he has not been imaged. His risk of carrying the mutation is 1/2, and an affected parent passes it to half of his children, so each child's risk is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

sections.title: Type IV collagen disease: Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease

blocks.text: Type IV collagen forms the sheet-like network of basement membranes. Each molecule is a triple helix of three alpha chains joined head to head through C-terminal noncollagenous (NC1) domains. The embryonic glomerular basement membrane (GBM) is built from alpha-1, alpha-1, alpha-2 molecules; as glomeruli mature, podocytes switch to an alpha-3, alpha-4, alpha-5 network that is more cross-linked and more resistant to proteases. The same alpha-3, 4, 5 network occurs in the cochlea, the lens capsule, and the retina. COL4A3 and COL4A4 lie together on chromosome 2, and COL4A5 lies on the X chromosome.

The three chains must assemble together, so a defect in any one prevents the whole alpha-3, 4, 5 network from forming. The GBM keeps the embryonic network, which is adequate at first but degrades under years of filtration pressure. It becomes irregularly thinned and thickened, and on electron microscopy the lamina densa splits into layers with a basket-weave pattern. Red cells leak through the breaks, so persistent microscopic hematuria, with episodes of gross hematuria, is the earliest sign, followed by proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and progressive loss of GFR. Defective basement membranes in the ear and eye cause sensorineural hearing loss, starting at high frequencies in late childhood, and anterior lenticonus (a conical bulge of the thin lens capsule) with dot-and-fleck retinopathy.

About 80% of families are X-linked (COL4A5), about 15% autosomal recessive (both alleles of COL4A3 or COL4A4), and a few autosomal dominant. Hemizygous males with X-linked disease have no normal alpha-5 chain and usually reach kidney failure as young adults. Heterozygous females are mosaics because of random X inactivation: GBM segments made by podocytes using the normal X are intact, so most have hematuria and only a minority progress. A normal transplanted kidney presents alpha-3, 4, 5 chains the recipient has never made, so a few recipients make anti-GBM alloantibodies, mainly against alpha-5 in X-linked disease and alpha-3 in recessive disease.

Thin basement membrane disease (TBMD) results from a heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutation. The normal allele supplies enough chain to build a complete but uniformly thin GBM (about 150 to 250 nm, against about 300 to 400 nm in adults) without splitting. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern and causes persistent isolated microscopic hematuria with normal kidney function and no ear or eye disease, although a minority of carriers later develop proteinuria and declining GFR.

Progressive to kidney failure, earliest in males
blocks.caption: Hematuria alone does not separate the two; progression, splitting of the GBM, and extrarenal findings do.

Each has a 50% risk of being heterozygous

blocks.predict: A man with X-linked Alport syndrome and an unaffected woman have children. What is the risk for each son and each daughter?
blocks.explain: Sons receive his Y chromosome and are unaffected. Every daughter receives his mutant X and is heterozygous; most will have hematuria, and some will progress, depending on X inactivation in their podocytes.

sections.title: VHL loss, HIF, and clear cell renal carcinoma

blocks.text: Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) has an oxygen-regulated alpha subunit and a constant beta subunit. In normal oxygen, prolyl hydroxylases use O2, Fe2+, and alpha-ketoglutarate to hydroxylate prolines on HIF-alpha. The VHL protein (pVHL), the substrate-recognition part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, binds hydroxylated HIF-alpha and polyubiquitinates it, and the proteasome destroys it within minutes. In hypoxia hydroxylation stops, HIF-alpha pairs with HIF-beta, and the dimer activates VEGF, PDGF-beta, TGF-alpha, erythropoietin (EPO), the glucose transporter GLUT1, and glycolytic enzymes.

blocks.title: From VHL loss to a vascular clear cell tumor
steps: First hit: 3p deletion or VHL mutation
Second hit removes the remaining VHL allele
Hydroxylated HIF-alpha is no longer ubiquitinated
HIF accumulates as if the cell were hypoxic
VEGF and PDGF build dense, fragile vessels
TGF-alpha drives growth; EPO may raise hematocrit
Glycogen and lipid storage give clear cytoplasm
blocks.caption: The tumor cell senses normal oxygen as hypoxia; every feature of the tumor follows from constant HIF activity.

blocks.text: VHL, on chromosome 3p25, is a tumor suppressor: one functional copy is enough, so a tumor requires loss of both copies (the Knudson two-hit model). Without pVHL the cell behaves as though permanently hypoxic. VEGF and PDGF build a dense network of thin-walled vessels, so clear cell carcinoma is highly vascular, bleeds (hematuria and a hemorrhagic yellow cut surface), and tends to grow into the renal vein. TGF-alpha stimulates proliferation through the EGF receptor, tumor EPO can cause paraneoplastic polycythemia, and the shift toward glycolysis and lipid storage contributes to cytoplasm full of glycogen and lipid that dissolve during processing. The tumor arises from proximal tubule epithelium and accounts for about 70 to 80% of renal cell carcinomas.

In sporadic clear cell carcinoma both hits are somatic and must occur in the same cell, usually deletion of one 3p copy plus mutation or promoter hypermethylation of the other, so the typical patient is an older adult (about 60s) with a single unilateral tumor; smoking, obesity, and hypertension raise the risk. In von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant, about 1 in 36,000) the first hit is germline. Every cell already lacks one copy, and one somatic event anywhere produces a tumor, so renal cysts and carcinomas are multiple, bilateral, and appear decades earlier. The extrarenal tumors form the same way in other tissues; hemangioblastomas, like clear cell carcinoma, are richly vascular and can secrete EPO.

blocks.title: Sporadic clear cell carcinoma and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
rows: Hemangioblastomas of cerebellum, spinal cord, retina; pheochromocytoma; pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors; endolymphatic sac tumors
blocks.caption: The gene and pathway are identical; only the timing of the first hit differs.

blocks.predict: A biopsy from a normal kidney region of a patient with a germline VHL mutation is examined. Would its tubular cells overexpress VEGF?
blocks.explain: No. Each cell still has one normal VHL allele, which makes enough pVHL to destroy HIF-alpha. VEGF rises only in cells that lose the second allele, which is why tumors are discrete even though every cell carries the mutation.
blocks.check: The two-hit paragraph and the first steps of the flow.

sections.title: Wilms tumor genetics: WT1 at 11p13 and imprinting at 11p15

blocks.text: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common primary renal malignancy of children, usually presenting at 2 to 5 years as a large unilateral flank mass. It arises from persistent embryonic metanephric blastema (nephrogenic rests) and recapitulates nephrogenesis: the classic triphasic histology is blastema, stroma, and epithelium forming abortive tubules and glomeruli. Most cases are sporadic; about 10% occur in a syndrome, and the syndromes identify the genes.

WT1, on 11p13, encodes a zinc-finger transcription factor of the intermediate mesoderm. It is required for metanephric mesenchyme to convert into nephron epithelium in response to signals from the ureteric bud, for podocyte differentiation and maintenance, and for early gonadal development, including regulation of SRY. Without WT1, blastema fails to differentiate and keeps proliferating, and podocytes and gonads are also affected. WT1 acts as a tumor suppressor but is mutated in only a minority (about 10 to 20%) of sporadic Wilms tumors.

WAGR syndrome is a germline deletion of 11p13 that removes one copy of WT1 and the neighboring PAX6. PAX6 haploinsufficiency causes aniridia, WT1 loss causes genitourinary anomalies (cryptorchidism, hypospadias) and a Wilms tumor risk of about 50%, and loss of other genes in the deletion contributes to intellectual disability. The tumor itself needs a second, somatic hit in the remaining WT1 allele, a two-hit pattern like VHL. Denys-Drash syndrome is caused instead by a heterozygous missense mutation in a WT1 zinc finger whose product interferes with the normal protein (a dominant negative effect). Because function falls further than with simple loss of one copy, podocytes fail early (diffuse mesangial sclerosis with nephrotic syndrome in infancy and progression to kidney failure), gonadal development fails (46,XY disorder of sex development), and Wilms tumor risk is about 90%.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) involves a different locus, the imprinted cluster at 11p15.5. IGF2, a fetal growth factor, is expressed only from the paternal allele; H19 (a noncoding RNA) and CDKN1C (the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p57) are expressed only from the maternal allele. Defects that raise IGF2 or lower CDKN1C cause overgrowth: macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia, visceromegaly including large kidneys, and neonatal hypoglycemia from islet hyperplasia and hyperinsulinism. Embryonal tumor risk (Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma) is about 5 to 10% overall, highest with paternal uniparental disomy or gain of methylation at the H19 and IGF2 imprinting center.

blocks.title: Syndromes that predispose to Wilms tumor
rows: Haploinsufficiency; second WT1 hit in tumor
Diffuse mesangial sclerosis, early nephrotic syndrome, 46,XY disorder of sex development
Macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia, organomegaly, neonatal hypoglycemia
blocks.caption: 11p13 lesions damage a differentiation gene; 11p15 lesions change the dose of growth genes.

blocks.title: Worked example: imprinting dosage in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
blocks.text: Normally a cell expresses one dose of IGF2 (from the paternal 11p15) and one dose of CDKN1C (from the maternal 11p15). Suppose a postzygotic error leaves some cells with two paternal copies of 11p15 and no maternal copy (paternal uniparental disomy). Those cells express two doses of IGF2 and no CDKN1C: growth signaling doubles and a brake on the cell cycle is lost. Because the error happens after fertilization, only some cells carry it, so overgrowth is patchy, which explains hemihyperplasia. No DNA sequence is mutated, yet expression is abnormal, which is why imprinting disorders need methylation testing rather than sequencing alone.

sections.title: Tuberous sclerosis: hamartin, tuberin, mTOR, and angiomyolipoma

blocks.text: mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) is a serine/threonine kinase complex that couples growth factor and nutrient availability to cell growth. Active mTORC1 phosphorylates S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 to increase protein synthesis, promotes lipid synthesis, and suppresses autophagy. Its direct activator is Rheb, a small GTPase that stimulates mTORC1 only when bound to GTP.

Hamartin (TSC1, chromosome 9q34) and tuberin (TSC2, chromosome 16p13.3) form a complex in which hamartin stabilizes tuberin and tuberin acts as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for Rheb, converting active Rheb-GTP to inactive Rheb-GDP. The complex integrates signals: growth factors acting through PI3K and Akt phosphorylate and inhibit tuberin, releasing mTORC1, whereas low cellular energy activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which activates tuberin and slows growth. Loss of either protein leaves Rheb in the GTP state and mTORC1 constitutively active, so cells grow and proliferate without the normal signals.

blocks.title: Loss of the TSC brake on mTOR
steps: Germline TSC1 or TSC2 mutation; somatic second hit
Hamartin-tuberin complex lost
No GAP activity: Rheb stays bound to GTP
mTORC1 constitutively active
Protein and lipid synthesis rise; autophagy falls
Hamartomas: angiomyolipomas, tubers, angiofibromas
blocks.caption: Tuberin normally switches Rheb off; without it, mTORC1 runs regardless of growth factor or energy status.

blocks.text: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is autosomal dominant with high penetrance but very variable expression, and about two-thirds of cases are new mutations; TSC2 mutations generally cause more severe disease. Lesions follow the two-hit pattern, forming where a somatic event removes the second allele. Hamartomas appear in the brain (cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytomas, with seizures and intellectual disability), skin (hypomelanotic ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas), heart (rhabdomyomas that often regress after birth), and lung (lymphangioleiomyomatosis in women).

Renal angiomyolipomas develop in most adults with TSC (about 70 to 80%) and are usually multiple and bilateral. They belong to the perivascular epithelioid cell tumor family and contain thick-walled dysplastic blood vessels with poor elastic tissue, smooth muscle, and mature fat. The abnormal vessel walls form aneurysms that can rupture into the retroperitoneum, and enlarging tumors replace parenchyma, so renal disease is a leading cause of death in adults with TSC. Fat is a diagnostic clue because it is rare in renal cell carcinoma. Renal cysts are also common, and because TSC2 lies directly beside PKD1 on 16p13.3, a contiguous deletion of both genes causes severe polycystic disease in infancy. Sporadic angiomyolipomas are usually single and occur most often in middle-aged women.

sections.title: Cystinuria: a dibasic amino acid transport defect

blocks.text: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 99% of filtered amino acids through apical transporters grouped by substrate class. Cystine, the disulfide-linked dimer of two cysteines, shares one transporter with the dibasic amino acids ornithine, lysine, and arginine. This transporter, system b0,+, is a heterodimer of a heavy subunit, rBAT (gene SLC3A1, chromosome 2), and a light subunit, b0,+AT (gene SLC7A9, chromosome 19). It takes up luminal cystine and dibasic amino acids in exchange for intracellular neutral amino acids, and the same transporter works in the small intestinal brush border.

Cystinuria is usually autosomal recessive: loss of both alleles of either gene abolishes the transporter, so all four amino acids appear in the urine in large amounts. Ornithine, lysine, and arginine are soluble and are lost harmlessly, and intestinal malabsorption causes no deficiency because these amino acids are still absorbed as di- and tripeptides by the separate peptide transporter PepT1. Cystine is the problem because it is the least soluble amino acid, about 250 mg/L at pH 7, lower in acidic urine, and rising steeply only above about pH 7.5. A homozygous patient excretes several hundred to more than 1,000 mg/day, compared with normal excretion under about 30 mg/day, which exceeds solubility in an ordinary urine volume. Some SLC7A9 heterozygotes excrete moderately increased cystine but rarely form stones.

blocks.title: From transporter defect to cystine stones
steps: Both alleles of SLC3A1 or SLC7A9 defective
Apical b0,+ transporter absent in proximal tubule
Cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine stay in tubular fluid
Cystine exceeds its solubility, especially in acidic urine
Hexagonal crystals nucleate and aggregate
Recurrent radiopaque stones, sometimes staghorn
blocks.caption: Four amino acids are lost, but only cystine precipitates.

blocks.text: Stones begin in childhood or young adulthood and recur. They are radiopaque because of their sulfur content, though less dense than calcium stones, and may fill the collecting system as staghorn calculi. Urine microscopy shows flat hexagonal crystals, which are pathognomonic and are best seen in concentrated, acidic first-morning urine. The cyanide-nitroprusside screen detects excess cystine: cyanide reduces each cystine to two cysteines, and their free sulfhydryl groups react with nitroprusside to give a red-purple color. The screen is also positive in homocystinuria, whose urine contains the disulfide homocystine, so a positive result is confirmed by quantitative urine amino acid measurement.

blocks.title: Cystinuria and look-alike disorders
rows: Apical b0,+ transporter (cystine and dibasic amino acids), kidney and gut
Cystine crystals inside cells; Fanconi syndrome, corneal crystals, kidney failure
Neutral amino acid transporter (B0AT1), kidney and gut
Tryptophan loss; pellagra-like rash and ataxia
Positive nitroprusside test without a transport defect; thrombosis, lens dislocation
blocks.caption: Cystinuria is a membrane transport defect; cystinosis is a lysosomal storage defect.

blocks.predict: One child has cystinuria and another has cystinosis. Which would you expect to have glycosuria, phosphaturia, and generalized aminoaciduria, and why?
blocks.explain: The child with cystinosis. Cystine trapped in proximal tubule lysosomes injures the cells and impairs all their reabsorptive transporters (Fanconi syndrome). In cystinuria only one transporter is missing, so glucose, phosphate, and other amino acids are reabsorbed normally.
blocks.check: The look-alike table and the description of system b0,+.

blocks.text: Glycosphingolipids are ceramide-based membrane lipids carrying sugar chains. Lysosomes degrade them by removing sugars one at a time from the outer end, each step catalyzed by a specific acid hydrolase. Alpha-galactosidase A, encoded by GLA on Xq22, removes the terminal alpha-linked galactose from globotriaosylceramide (Gb3, also called ceramide trihexoside), leaving lactosylceramide.

When the enzyme is deficient, Gb3 and its deacylated form, lyso-Gb3, accumulate in lysosomes of vascular endothelium and smooth muscle, podocytes and tubular cells, cardiomyocytes, dorsal root ganglion neurons and small nerve fibers, sweat glands, and corneal epithelium. On electron microscopy the stored lipid forms concentric lamellated inclusions (zebra bodies), and on light microscopy podocytes look foamy and vacuolated. Lyso-Gb3 also promotes endothelial dysfunction, smooth muscle proliferation, and fibrosis, so tissue injury extends beyond the space the lipid occupies.

blocks.title: Fabry manifestations explained by storage site
rows: Small sensory fibers, dorsal root ganglia
Burning pain in hands and feet (acroparesthesias) from childhood, crises with fever, heat, or exercise
Angiokeratomas, clustered between umbilicus and knees
Proteinuria, concentrating defect, progressive kidney failure
Left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias, early stroke
blocks.caption: One enzyme defect produces findings in skin, nerve, eye, kidney, heart, and brain because Gb3 accumulates wherever it is made.

blocks.text: Kidney disease follows a sequence. Podocyte storage causes proteinuria, often beginning in the 20s in males with classic disease; tubular storage impairs urine concentration; and progressive glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis lead to kidney failure, classically in the 30s to 50s. The urine sediment may contain lipid-laden cells and fat droplets that show a Maltese cross under polarized light.

Fabry disease is X-linked. Hemizygous males with classic mutations have little or no enzyme activity and the full picture from childhood. Heterozygous females are mosaics because of random X inactivation, and many develop symptoms, usually later and milder but sometimes severe when inactivation is skewed toward the mutant X. For this reason the inheritance is better described as X-linked than strictly recessive, and the pedigree rules match those in C02. Enzyme activity confirms the diagnosis in males but may be normal in heterozygous females, who need GLA testing. Later-onset variants with residual enzyme activity can present only with cardiac or renal disease in adulthood. Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome are the classic X-linked lysosomal storage diseases.

integration.text: These disorders fall into four mechanistic groups. Structural protein defects (polycystins, fibrocystin, type IV collagen) damage the tubule or basement membrane and show the same lesion wherever the protein is used, which is why PKD brings liver cysts and aneurysms and Alport brings deafness and lens defects. Tumor suppressor syndromes (VHL, WT1, TSC) follow the two-hit model, so inherited forms give early, multiple, bilateral lesions and sporadic forms give single lesions later in life; the exceptions are dominant negative WT1 in Denys-Drash, where one mutant allele already impairs podocytes and gonads, and BWS, where gene dosage changes through imprinting without any sequence mutation. Transport defects (cystinuria) act through solubility, and lysosomal storage (Fabry) acts through progressive cell injury.

The kidney links each group to other Part I disciplines: cilia and cAMP signaling (cell biology), basement membrane collagen and anti-GBM immunity (biochemistry and immunology), HIF and EPO (physiology of oxygen sensing), mTOR and growth signaling (biochemistry), amino acid transport (renal physiology), and sphingolipid degradation (biochemistry). The limits are real: penetrance and expression vary, many sporadic tumors carry other mutations, and quoted percentages differ between sources, so pedigree risks assume complete penetrance unless stated otherwise.

summary: ADPKD: PKD1 (chromosome 16, polycystin-1, about 85%, more severe) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, polycystin-2); ciliary Ca2+ falls, cAMP rises, cysts proliferate and secrete fluid; liver cysts, berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse.
ARPKD: PKHD1 (chromosome 6, fibrocystin); infant collecting duct cysts, oligohydramnios with Potter sequence, and congenital hepatic fibrosis.

Dominant pedigrees are vertical with male-to-male transmission and 50% risk per child; recessive pedigrees are horizontal with 25% risk, and an unaffected sibling of an affected child has a 2/3 carrier risk.

Alport syndrome: a defect in any alpha-3, 4, or 5 chain (usually X-linked COL4A5) prevents the mature GBM network, giving a split basket-weave GBM, hematuria to kidney failure, hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus.
Thin basement membrane disease: one mutant COL4A3 or COL4A4 allele gives a uniformly thin GBM and isolated hematuria with usually normal function.

VHL (3p25) targets hydroxylated HIF-alpha for destruction; loss of both copies stabilizes HIF and drives VEGF, PDGF, TGF-alpha, and EPO in clear cell carcinoma; a germline first hit gives early bilateral tumors, hemangioblastomas, and pheochromocytoma.

WT1 (11p13) loss causes Wilms tumor with genitourinary defects: WAGR by deletion with PAX6 (aniridia), Denys-Drash by dominant negative mutation (mesangial sclerosis, 46,XY disorder of sex development).
Beckwith-Wiedemann: 11p15.5 imprinting defects increase IGF2 and reduce CDKN1C, causing overgrowth and embryonal tumors including Wilms tumor.
TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) loss removes GAP control of Rheb, so mTORC1 stays active; angiomyolipomas (vessels, smooth muscle, fat) and renal cysts follow.

Cystinuria: autosomal recessive loss of the b0,+ transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine gives hexagonal cystine stones and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test; Fabry: X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency stores Gb3, causing angiokeratomas, painful neuropathy, hypohidrosis, and progressive kidney failure.

verify: Gene fractions vary by source: PKD1 about 78 to 85% of ADPKD, X-linked COL4A5 about 80% of Alport, WT1 mutation in about 10 to 20% of sporadic Wilms tumors; values here are stated as approximate.

ADPKD incidence (1 in 400 to 1,000), ARPKD incidence (about 1 in 20,000), the derived ARPKD carrier frequency (about 1 in 70), and VHL syndrome incidence (about 1 in 36,000) are commonly quoted estimates; confirm the figures NABNE expects.
Wilms tumor risks (about 50% in WAGR, about 90% in Denys-Drash, about 5 to 10% embryonal tumor risk in Beckwith-Wiedemann) differ between sources and Beckwith-Wiedemann subtypes.
Nomenclature is changing: many authorities now classify heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 carriers (thin basement membrane disease) as autosomal dominant Alport syndrome; confirm which term NABNE uses.
Cystine solubility (about 250 mg/L at pH 7) and normal versus cystinuric excretion values are quoted with some variation; the nitroprusside positivity threshold is not given here.
Normal adult GBM thickness (about 300 to 400 nm) and the thin membrane range (about 150 to 250 nm) vary with laboratory method and sex.

The relative contributions of reduced ciliary Ca2+ and raised cAMP in ADPKD cystogenesis are a working model rather than a settled mechanism; the statement that polycystins sense luminal flow is presented as likely, not proven.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: pedigree-patterns (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked pedigrees side by side) and hif-vhl-pathway (HIF-alpha hydroxylation and VHL ubiquitination in normoxia versus VHL loss).
